conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I know you’ve been having abdominal pain—can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse over the past few days. It started in the upper right side and now it’s more in the lower left. I’ve also been nauseous and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned this happened before recently—was that related to your pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, last time they thought it was my chronic pancreatitis flaring up, or maybe a side effect from an antibiotic I was on. But I couldn’t get the new medicine they prescribed because of insurance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. And I see you were in a car accident recently—how are you feeling from that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my car was totaled. I got checked out at another hospital. I still have some pain across my lower belly from the seatbelt and my knee is bruised, but nothing broken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show? Is it my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, your pancreas looks normal on the scan. But we did find a partial blockage in your small bowel—called a partial small-bowel obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A blockage? How does that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to scar tissue from your past C-section. That can cause adhesions—bands of tissue that pull on the bowel and cause a kink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that could happen. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but yours is partial, not complete. That means some fluid and gas can still pass. We don’t think you need surgery—we’ll treat it with bowel rest, IV fluids, and close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. What does bowel rest mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means no food or drink by mouth for now. We’ll give you fluids and nutrients through your IV. Once your bowel starts moving again—like passing gas or having a bowel movement—we can slowly restart your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did pass some gas earlier. Does that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign! It means your bowel is starting to work again. We’ll keep an eye on your symptoms and repeat an X-ray tomorrow to check progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain? I’ve been using the nitroglycerin under my tongue, but it helps only a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV fluids and Dilaudid for pain. We’ll also continue your home meds for GERD and anxiety, since those can make symptoms worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also had headaches lately, with nausea. I don’t usually get them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. You’re on medications that can help with migraines, like imipramine and trazodone. We’ll keep those going and follow up on the headaches after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your X-ray from this morning. There’s some contrast now in your colon, which means your bowel is moving again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. You’ve also had a bowel movement, which is another positive sign. We’re going to start you on clear liquids—like broth and apple juice—and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take it step by step. If you do well with clear liquids, we’ll advance to soft foods tomorrow. The key is not to rush it—otherwise, the blockage could come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the fibroids the scan mentioned? I didn’t know I had those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed your uterus has fibroids—noncancerous growths. They’re common and often don’t cause symptoms. But if you have heavy periods or pelvic pain, you should mention it to your gynecologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do have some pelvic discomfort sometimes. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The scan also showed extra veins in the pelvis, which could suggest pelvic congestion syndrome. That’s something to discuss with your doctor later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll bring it up. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve been tolerating a full diet, your pain is much better, and labs are normal. We’re planning to discharge you this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your regular medications. We’re adding a short course of Percocet for breakthrough pain—only 10 pills, no refills, because of your allergy to certain medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—I’m allergic to Sulfa, Protonix, Risperdal, and Ambien. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also, follow up with your primary care doctor and gastroenterologist. They’ll help manage your chronic pancreatitis and bowel issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about another blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The risk is there because of the adhesions, but eating slowly, staying hydrated, and avoiding constipation can help prevent it. If you have severe pain, vomiting, or can’t pass gas, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And what about the headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your current meds. If the headaches continue, your doctor might adjust your treatment. Stress and poor sleep can trigger them, so try to rest and manage anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been through a lot lately—the accident, the pain, not being able to get my meds. It’s been hard on my mental health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your depression and PTSD are important. Keep in touch with your therapist. These flare-ups can be both physical and emotional.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be able to go home in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid driving after the accident and all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. If you’re still on pain meds, don’t drive. Once you’re off them and feeling stable, it should be okay. But if you’re anxious, consider talking to a counselor before getting back behind the wheel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call your doctor if anything changes.

conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. ERCP carries a risk of triggering pancreatitis, and since the imaging doesn’t show a clear target, your GI doctor doesn’t think it’s worth the risk right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. So I just keep managing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll keep you on your usual Dilaudid for pain, Reglan for nausea, and your other meds. We’re encouraging you to try advancing your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today? Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less sharp. I had some toast this morning—no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your lipase was slightly elevated yesterday but not in the range for acute pancreatitis. It’s actually come down today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an acute flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not based on labs or imaging. Your pain seems to be part of your chronic condition. We’re not seeing new damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve lost about 10 pounds because I’m so afraid to eat. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, yes. Malnutrition can make everything worse. We want you to keep trying small, bland meals. Maybe add in some protein like scrambled eggs or yogurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. What about my anemia? My hematocrit is low again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your Hct is around 31, which is your baseline. No sign of bleeding, and you haven’t had a bowel movement since admission, so we’re not worried about active loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my mental health meds—are they still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your fluoxetine, clonazepam, imipramine, and trazodone. It’s important to keep those steady, especially with everything going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I have the final results. The MRCP shows no evidence of chronic pancreatitis or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction. The pancreas looks structurally normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still have pain. What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the pain isn’t from visible damage or blockage. The reduced fluid output is still there, but it’s not clear how much that contributes. Your GI doctor wants to see you soon to discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m being discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your condition is stable. We’re sending you home with Dilaudid for pain until your appointment. No changes to your other medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more tests for now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your doctor will decide if anything else is needed. Focus on eating well, staying hydrated, and keeping that follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad I’m not having another ERCP, but I hope we figure this out soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep working on it. You’re doing the right thing by staying in close contact with your GI team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. I understand you passed out at your psychologist’s office today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I stood up and everything went dark. I woke up on the floor. I’ve done this before when I’m sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned dizziness and nausea before it happened. Is that part of your usual abdominal pain episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nausea is always there when my stomach pain flares. It’s in my upper left side, worse after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve lost about 10 pounds recently without trying?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because I can’t eat much. Every time I do, the pain gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you manage the pain and get your nutrition up. You also had a syncopal episode in the ER two days ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same thing—lightheaded, then blacked out. I didn’t hit my head either time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, no injury. We did a chest X-ray to check for anything serious. It was clear—no pneumonia or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a cold lately, but it’s mild. Is that why I fainted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. When you’re dehydrated or not eating well, standing up can drop your blood pressure. That, plus a mild URI, could explain it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. Your vitals are stable. We’ll keep an IV for fluids and start pain meds to help you eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to some pain meds, like hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll avoid those. We’ll use alternatives and monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. I had some toast and kept it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep encouraging small meals. Your urine test came back—no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about a UTI. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and no signs of bleeding or anemia worsening. We’ll keep checking your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well with oral intake, but you’re still not eating like at home. Your GI doctor wants you to stay until you’re back to your baseline diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go home, but I know I’m not ready. The pain’s still there, just less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focused on getting you stable. We also need to make sure the fainting doesn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sitting up slowly. No dizziness yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep doing that. We’ll continue IV fluids until you’re eating enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing your recent MRCP again with radiology to make sure we didn’t miss anything with your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many scans. None have shown clear pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Some show decreased pancreatic fluid, but no definite chronic pancreatitis. We’re considering other causes for your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be something else? My stomach just feels so sensitive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re looking at biliary tract issues too. But for now, we’re managing symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two days of improved intake. That’s great. But you’re still losing weight unintentionally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m trying. I just don’t have an appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line tomorrow so we can start nutritional support through the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me gain weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it will give your body the calories and nutrients it needs while your stomach heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just got confirmation—the PICC line will be placed tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very. It’s a small tube in your arm vein, guided by ultrasound. We’ll check with a chest X-ray after to make sure it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully this morning. The chest X-ray shows it’s in the right position—tip in the SVC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel a thing. Is the nutrition starting now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting parenteral nutrition. It will help you regain strength and weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. This will help with that. We’ll monitor your labs closely for any imbalances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. You’ve had three meals today without nausea. Pain is mild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually felt hungry this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. We’ll keep the PICC for now, but you’re on track to go home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do you think?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow, if you keep this up. We’ll make sure you can eat consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Any dizziness when standing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been careful. I feel much more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That means your hydration and nutrition are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had another good day with meals. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What about the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will stay in for now. You’ll get home nutrition support and follow up with GI and nutrition services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for monitoring and eventual removal. We’ll coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue managing it with safe meds. Your GI doctor will review imaging again and may suggest next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fainting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As long as you stay hydrated and eat regularly, it’s unlikely to return. But if it happens again, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up with the diet, take meds as prescribed, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad I didn’t hit my head when I fell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and no new injuries. Just take it slow when standing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing that. No dizziness at all today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re ready to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m feeling hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best sign of all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my left breast has been sore for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lump, you said? And it’s not worse with movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lump, and it’s constant. Not painful, just uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll note it. Please follow up with your PCP for a breast exam, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s what we’re here for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hearing—I read lips, so I catch most of what you say.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure to face you and speak clearly. Your care team knows about your hearing loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. It makes a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want you to understand everything. Take your time going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. I know you’re in pain, so let’s get you settled first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s sharp pain in my upper belly, goes to my back. Worse when I eat. I think it’s my pancreas again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lipase was elevated in the ER, which supports that. We’ll keep you NPO for now—no food or drink by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. I’ve been through this before. But I’m nauseous. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll give you IV fluids and medication for nausea and pain. You already got Dilaudid in the ER, and we’ll continue that as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m also anxious—this pain makes it worse. I take clonazepam at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your meds. You can have your clonazepam as scheduled. We’ll make sure your anxiety is managed too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I read lips, so please face me when you speak. And I’m hard of hearing—thank you for speaking clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. I’ll always face you and speak slowly. We’ll make sure all staff know your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was supposed to talk about an ERCP soon. Is that still happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. Kim’s GI team saw you today. They’ve scheduled your ERCP for next week as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I hope it helps. I’ve had these flare-ups since my sphincter of Oddi dysfunction was diagnosed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why ERCP might help—to check the sphincter and possibly do a sphincterotomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need an interpreter for the procedure? I use ASL.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve noted that. A female ASL interpreter will be arranged for your ERCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot. I feel better already knowing there’s a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some ache, but not as sharp. Nausea is less too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs this morning show your lipase is coming down—from 150 to 106. That means your pancreas is calming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? Can I try drinking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry. But I’ll go slow. Last time I rushed, I got sick again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart. We’ll monitor you closely. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable. No need for transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia before. It’s been chronic. I’ll follow up with my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your primary team can manage that. For now, focus on healing your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after the clear liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No nausea. I had broth and juice, and my stomach feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll switch you to a low-fat solid diet—small portions. That’s easier on your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know the drill. No fats, small meals. I’ve learned the hard way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll also switch your pain med from IV to oral—same Dilaudid, but by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take it as needed? I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2 mg every 4 hours as needed. We’ll watch for side effects, but you’re alert and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made great progress. You’ve tolerated the diet, and your pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you. You’ll take Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, but use it sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds—can I restart them all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds are continued—clonazepam, fluoxetine, ranitidine, the others. We’ve sent prescriptions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ERCP is next week. I have the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Dr. Kim’s team will see you. Remember, a female ASL interpreter will be there for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything. I feel much better and ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest at home, stick to low-fat meals, and call if pain worsens or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for respecting my hearing needs. It made a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your care team will follow up with you. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be in touch. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re discharged. Nurse will give you instructions and help you leave shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be looking after you tonight. I see you came in with worsening abdominal pain and nausea since your last discharge. Can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain came back about three days ago—same spot, upper middle abdomen. It’s sharp and gets worse after eating. I haven’t been able to keep food down for two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your last bowel movement was today—was it normal in color and consistency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was normal. No diarrhea or constipation. But I’m really worried—could this be pancreatitis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility, given your history. But your lab work shows your amylase is 99—within normal range—and no signs of infection. Your symptoms suggest your sphincter of Oddi might be spasming again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not pancreatitis this time? But it feels just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can feel very similar. But since your enzyme levels are stable and you’ve had recurrent issues, we’ve scheduled an ERCP tomorrow morning to check the bile duct and possibly dilate the ampulla to help with drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before. Is it safe to do it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s routine. You already have a sphincterotomy from before, so we’ll use a balloon to gently widen the opening again. No stones were seen on imaging, so we don’t expect complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will I be asleep during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under sedation, so you’ll be very relaxed and won’t feel anything. The procedure takes about 30 to 45 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The ERCP is done. We dilated the ampulla successfully, and bile flow improved right away. No stones or blockages were found. The ducts look clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Does that mean the pain should go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect it to improve. You’re already saying you feel better, and you haven’t had nausea since the procedure. We’ll start you on clear liquids and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the clear diet well, so we’re upgrading you to a regular diet. Your vitals are stable, and your abdomen is soft and not tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today, likely within the next few hours. We’ll make sure you can eat without pain and give you updated prescriptions, including a stool softener to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge instructions are ready. No changes to your usual medications except adding docusate and senna. Keep taking your hydrocodone only if needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I still need to follow up with my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same plan—follow up with Dr. ___ in one week. They’ll decide if you need another procedure later. In the meantime, call if pain worsens or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already. I’m glad we did this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You’re doing well. We’ll have you out of here soon. Rest at home and take it easy for the next day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any new pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling okay. A little tired, but the pain is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The sedation can linger a bit. Keep someone with you tonight, and don’t drive until tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are signed. You’re cleared to go home now. Take care, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted for abdominal pain. Can you tell me about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea? Vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nauseous, yes. But no vomiting. I haven’t eaten much—only a little yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you’re not taking your Dilaudid at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’m used to it. But I’m worried—could this be another pancreatitis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as last time. After the ERCP, it got better. But now it’s back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we know this is recurrent. We’ll treat it supportively—IV fluids, pain control, and anti-nausea meds. Once you’re stable, we’ll slowly restart your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your repeat lipase dropped to 86 this morning—trending down. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: Good. Also stay hydrated and keep up with your mental health meds. Stress can worsen symptoms.

conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Abdomen is soft, only mild tenderness. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. Will I need more tests after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I taking when I leave?

conversation_lines.text: And pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment next week. I’ll tell them about the constipation and fissure too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid any foods completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-fat, bland foods for now. Avoid alcohol, fried foods, and heavy meals. Small, frequent meals are best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll keep a food diary like my GI doctor suggested.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent idea. That can help identify triggers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for reminding me. I’ll make sure all your providers know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you. The nurse will go over instructions and get you set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I’ll follow up and take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Take it easy, and we’ll see how things go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with abdominal pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same pain—epigastric, radiating to my back. Feels just like my usual flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You haven’t been able to eat for two days and feel nauseated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I’ve been on IV fluids in the ER. Can I get something for the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue IV hydromorphone as needed. We’ve reviewed your labs—lipase is 111, which is mildly elevated but not high enough to confirm pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it’s always been like this—my lipase never goes super high. Doesn’t mean it’s not pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your liver tests and ultrasound are normal. No gallstones, no duct dilation. The pancreas looks unremarkable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had four ERCPs before. The last one showed sphincter issues. Why won’t they fix it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team reviewed your history. They don’t think sphincter of Oddi dysfunction is a valid diagnosis anymore. There’s no objective evidence it’s causing your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had multiple sphincterotomies. They helped before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But repeated procedures haven’t stopped the admissions. You’ve been here over 50 times in ten years. We need to think differently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re saying it’s all in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the pain is real. But it may not be from pancreatitis. Chronic pain can change how the gut works—called narcotic bowel or motility disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Motility disorder? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means your intestines aren’t moving food through normally. Pain, nausea, constipation—can all be part of it. Especially with long-term narcotic use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need the pain meds. The pain is unbearable without them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re suggesting a pain management referral. They help reduce reliance on narcotics and improve function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to go. I’ve tried before. It didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll respect your decision. But we do recommend a bowel regimen. We’ve started Miralax for constipation.

conversation_lines.text: Right. So improving gut motility might help break that cycle. We also tried Dexilant today for stomach acid, but you said it gave you a headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll keep you on high-dose ranitidine. No more PPIs unless you’re willing to try another time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound from yesterday was normal—no gallstones, no pancreas issues. That supports our thinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still hurt. Doesn’t the pain mean something’s wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It does. But sometimes pain persists even when scans look normal. That’s common in chronic pain syndromes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan? Just send me home with pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep treating symptoms. But we’re also focusing on long-term strategies—like improving gut motility and reducing narcotic dependence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want the pain to stop. I can’t keep living like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. A social worker will meet with you to offer support. And we encourage you to consider the pain clinic in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better today. You had some toast and tolerated it. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nausea is less. But I still have a dull ache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow or the next day. We want to make sure you can eat and manage pain with oral meds first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do whatever I need to. I just want to be out of here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a full meal yesterday and no vomiting. Your pain is much improved. We think you’re ready for discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But what about the ERCP I was supposed to have?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still scheduled as an outpatient. But the team doesn’t expect it to change your symptoms, given the lack of findings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I’ll go, just in case. My last one helped for a few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support your choice. But we want you to know—most experts now doubt sphincter of Oddi dysfunction is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating. You’re saying everything I’ve been treated for isn’t real?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. Your pain is real. But the cause may not be structural. It could be how your nerves and gut interact—called a functional disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what helps that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Things like stress management, meditation, yoga. There are mind-body programs that help retrain how the brain processes pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never tried that. Seems… different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is. But many patients find it helpful alongside medication. We can give you info if you’re interested.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe later. Right now, I just want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’ve been off IV meds, eating well, and your pain is minimal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I do if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oral hydromorphone as needed, stay hydrated, and try to eat small meals. If it’s severe or you can’t keep food down, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Miralax?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue it twice daily as needed. It helps keep your bowels moving, which may reduce pain episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up with GI is scheduled. They’ll discuss the ERCP. But we encourage you to also consider non-medication approaches long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if you need help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It’s hard to give up everything.

conversation_lines.text: We know. Small changes over time can make a big difference. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll take that with me.

conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night are stable. No infection, kidney function is good. We’re holding off imaging since your symptoms match prior flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No CT scan? I usually get one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history and stable labs, we don’t think it’s needed. No signs of complications. We’re focusing on symptom control and getting you back on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach still feels full. I haven’t eaten.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on clear liquids today. Also, your GI team suggested a gastric emptying study to check your motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. They take hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but this one’s important. It will help confirm how severe your gastroparesis is and guide long-term treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gastric emptying study is back. It shows 81% of food still in your stomach after four hours. That’s severely delayed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That explains the fullness. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on metoclopramide, but we’re switching back to erythromycin. It helps stomach emptying and may reduce pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on erythromycin before my last flare. But I had diarrhea with the higher dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start at 125 mg three times a day—the dose you tolerate. If diarrhea returns, we’ll adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Pain is down to a 4. I had toast and applesauce last night—no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll advance you to a regular diet today. Still on oral hydromorphone for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I only took one dose yesterday. I’d like to stop the strong painkillers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good goal. We’ll taper slowly. Long-term, we want to reduce reliance on narcotics, especially with your vulvodynia and chronic pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a problem, but it’s the only thing that works sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with your doctors to find alternatives—like nerve pain meds or behavioral strategies. You’re already on gabapentin and imipramine, which help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test came back negative. The diarrhea you had earlier wasn’t from an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it the erythromycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. We reduced the dose, and it’s resolved. You’re still on 125 mg TID, which seems to be working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to go back to IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—eating regular meals, pain under control. We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Small, low-fat meals—like bananas, rice, applesauce, toast. Stay on erythromycin and metoclopramide as prescribed. Use hydromorphone only if absolutely needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue clonazepam, venlafaxine, and the others as before. Your mental health is important—don’t skip doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your recent labs are good. Hemoglobin is a bit low at 11.1, but stable. No signs of infection or dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Also, chronic conditions and medications can affect it. We’re not concerned now, but your doctor may check it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’re walking, eating, and pain is minimal. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your GI doctor soon. They’ll help optimize your treatment and reduce flare-ups. We’re sending them all your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain management?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It’s hard when the pain hits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. That’s why follow-up is key. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’re tolerating food, pain is controlled, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What’s the discharge plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with prescriptions: erythromycin, metoclopramide, hydromorphone for breakthrough pain, and your usual meds for anxiety and depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only 20 tablets of hydromorphone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just for short-term use. Please work with your doctor to taper it. We’re also sending instructions on diet and symptom tracking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your GI doctor first. If it’s severe and you can’t reach them, go to the ER. But try to avoid frequent admissions—we want you stable at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thank you for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed. Your hearing aids are packed—don’t forget them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have them. Thanks for speaking clearly and facing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s part of good care. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ve reviewed your chart and wanted to talk with you about why you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been really nauseous for two days and threw up twice. I think it started when I switched from reglan to erythromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. You’re on a rotating schedule between those two for your gastroparesis. The ER team gave you fluids and some anti-nausea meds. Your labs look stable—no sign of infection or pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my pancreas again? That’s good. But I still feel awful. I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lipase was only slightly elevated, which doesn’t suggest acute pancreatitis. We think this is more likely a flare of your gastroparesis, possibly triggered by the medication change or stress on your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many of these episodes. Over fifty times in the hospital. I just want to get better faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re going to focus on controlling your nausea and pain while letting your stomach rest. You’ll stay on IV fluids for now and we’ll monitor how you tolerate small sips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I still take my erythromycin? I’m supposed to be on it this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on oral meds until you can keep fluids down. Once you’re stable, we’ll restart it with meals. We don’t want to overload your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My belly’s been sore, but not as bad as some times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows mild tenderness, but your abdomen is soft. No signs of obstruction or infection. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I sipped some apple juice last night and didn’t throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids today—broth, tea, maybe some gelatin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous it’ll come back. Last time I tried too fast and ended up worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. If you tolerate this phase, we’ll move to soft foods tomorrow. The goal is steady improvement, not rushing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. What about my pain? I’ve been using the hydromorphone, but I don’t want to depend on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team reviewed your case. They recommend increasing your gabapentin to help with nerve-related pain and reduce opioid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on imipramine and venlafaxine. Is it safe to increase gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we checked. Gabapentin is safe with your other meds. We’re not starting nortriptyline because of your other medications affecting heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You made it through clear liquids well. We’re switching you to a soft diet—mashed potatoes, applesauce, toast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That sounds amazing. Can I have some scrambled eggs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s start simple. If you do well, we can add eggs tomorrow. Also, your gabapentin has been increased to 600 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big jump. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Drowsiness or dizziness, especially at first. Let the nurse know if you feel unsteady. But it should help your pain over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your nausea has improved, and you’ve kept down soft foods. We’re going to restart your erythromycin with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I was worried about that. Last time I had diarrhea with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. If it causes issues, we can adjust the dose or switch back to reglan when it’s time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My anxiety’s been worse with all this. I’ve been using my clonazepam as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll keep supporting your mental health. Your prazosin and venlafaxine are continuing as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lab results from this morning show your kidney function is good, and your electrolytes are stable. Hemoglobin is a bit low but not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been tired. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It could also be from the recent illness and being on bed rest. As you eat more and get moving, your energy should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to walk a little today. Just to the bathroom by myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great idea. Start slow and let the nurse know if you feel dizzy. Staying active helps your digestion too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off IV fluids since yesterday—excellent. You’re maintaining hydration on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m drinking water and broth all day. My stomach feels less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also seeing your pain is better controlled with the higher gabapentin. You’ve only used hydromorphone twice in 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I’m finally turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s plan is to keep your current diet and meds. We’re focusing on full symptom control before discharge planning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking—do you think my pain is more from nerves than my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a mix. Your gastroparesis causes physical symptoms, but nerve sensitivity and stress can amplify pain. That’s why gabapentin helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been through a lot—PTSD, anxiety. It’s hard to separate what’s body and what’s mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We see it as all connected. Treating both helps you heal better. Your mental health meds are important—don’t stop them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking stronger. Your blood pressure is a bit low today—94 over 56—but you’re not dizzy. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stood up slow this morning. I’ve been drinking extra fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good job. That helps. Your labs this morning are all stable. Lipase is down to 48—back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no pancreatitis. Just my usual mess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. This was a gastroparesis and functional dyspepsia flare. We’re managing it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days of regular meals and no nausea. We’re considering discharge in the next day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue erythromycin with meals, take metoclopramide if nausea returns, and use hydromorphone only as needed—short supply to avoid overuse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with Dr. Patel like we planned. She’s helping with my motility issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep using gabapentin as prescribed. It will help reduce pain flares and your need for narcotics over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is set for tomorrow morning. We’ll finalize your meds and send instructions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But I’m scared it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might, but now we have a better plan—earlier use of anti-nausea meds, slower diet advancement, and gabapentin to manage pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll call my doctor before coming in, unless it’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want to avoid unnecessary admissions. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. Here’s your medication list and follow-up details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up with your mental health care too—your clonazepam, venlafaxine, prazosin, and imipramine are all continuing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll wear my hearing aids and keep using lip-reading. It helps me feel in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care of yourself. Call if symptoms return or worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening and helping me through this.

conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you doing at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doing well. Ate scrambled eggs this morning—no nausea. Still taking gabapentin and erythromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep it up. See you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. I’ve been walking every day. Feels good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for normal activity. Continue your meds as prescribed and follow up with Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call her office today. I’m feeling more hopeful this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: you were admitted with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Your symptoms improved with gabapentin up-titration, bowel rest, IV fluids, and gradual diet advancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were discharged home with a short supply of hydromorphone, continued erythromycin and metoclopramide for nausea, and increased gabapentin for pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll stick to the plan and follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Take care of your mental and physical health. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really appreciate the support.

conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started right after I restarted my erythromycin. It’s my typical pain—sharp, in the upper middle, and it makes me nauseous and vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that matches what we saw in the ER. Your lipase was high—682—which can happen with pancreatitis, but we need to check further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. It’s pancreatitis. I usually get Dilaudid every four hours, and it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain carefully. For now, we’re keeping you on IV fluids and giving you Dilaudid as needed. We’ll reassess how often you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also get really anxious during these episodes. I take Klonopin and Effexor—can I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your Klonopin and Effexor. We’re also monitoring your hearing—do you need me to face you when I speak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. And I don’t want any PPIs—they give me migraines. I told the nurse I’m allergic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We won’t give you any proton pump inhibitors. We’re using ranitidine instead, which is safe for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your lipase has dropped to 105, which is a good sign. Your blood sugar was low at 48, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low sugar? I didn’t feel shaky or confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No symptoms now, but we’re checking your glucose every six hours. We’re also sending tests to make sure there’s no insulin overproduction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be from my pancreas? I’ve had so many scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering that. But your past EUS didn’t show any growths. Still, we’ll follow up on this after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to order an MRCP today to check your pancreas and bile ducts. It’s a special MRI that helps us see those areas clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had MRCPs before. They were normal. Do we really need another?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because your symptoms and lipase are up again. We need to rule out pancreatitis or duct blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRCP was done yesterday. Good news—it shows no signs of pancreatitis. Your pancreas looks normal, and there’s no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my pain feels just like pancreatitis. How can the scan be normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible your pain is from gastroparesis—delayed stomach emptying. Vomiting and high lipase can happen with that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pancreatitis? But Dilaudid helps me. Why would I need it if it’s not severe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dilaudid can help with different kinds of pain. But we’re being cautious with opioids. We’re switching you to oral Dilaudid every six hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need it every four hours. That’s what works. And I usually get it prescribed when I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not discharging you on oral Dilaudid this time. Your pain is improving, and we want to avoid long-term opioid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m upset. I know my body. This is what helps. Why are you changing things?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you, and I’m not dismissing your experience. But we have to balance pain control with safety. We’ll keep adjusting as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your eosinophil count is up. It was normal when you came in. We’re not sure why yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Eosinophils? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be a sign of inflammation or allergy. Since you’re on erythromycin, we’re considering if it’s a reaction. We’ll follow it after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop the erythromycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you from IV to oral erythromycin. If the eosinophilia persists, your GI doctor can reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on full liquids. No pain reported. We’re going to try advancing you to a regular diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I still worry about the pain coming back when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have your regular medications, including metoclopramide and erythromycin. And you’ll follow up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose dropped again last night—to 62. Still no symptoms, but we’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t feel low. Is this dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it drops lower. We’re checking for insulinoma, but it’s unlikely given your history and past scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring and send more tests. After discharge, your PCP will follow up on your glucose and eosinophil count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on a regular diet since yesterday with no pain. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. But I’m still not happy about not getting Dilaudid to take home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your pain is controlled without it, and we’re concerned about dependency. We’ll rely on your regular meds and GI follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I might go to another hospital if I flare again. They give me what I need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hope you don’t have to. But your care team, including GI and social work, has discussed your concerns. We want you safe and supported.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re being discharged today. No abdominal pain, tolerating regular food, and your lipase is down. We believe this was a gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the MRCP was clear. The high lipase was likely from vomiting and gastroparesis. You’ll follow up with your GI doctor and PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the low sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a note to your doctors to check your glucose and repeat your CBC for the eosinophilia. But you’re safe to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.
